tools.title: Tools
tools.subtitle: A free toolbox for students: grade averages, networking, conversions and more. No account needed — everything runs in your browser.
tools.metaDescription: Free tools for students: weighted grade calculator, IPv4 subnet calculator, base converter, Base64 encoder and JWT decoder. No account, runs in your browser.
indexAbout: Freenote gathers small tools that come in handy as a student: compute a weighted average, check a subnet for a networking class, convert a number between bases or inspect a token. Each one has its own page, with an explanation and worked examples.
Every calculation runs directly in your browser: nothing is sent to a server, it is instant and free. No account is required to use them.

ipv4.name: IPv4 / subnet calculator (CIDR)
ipv4.short: Network address, broadcast, host range and mask from an IP and a CIDR.
ipv4.lead: Enter an IPv4 address and a mask (CIDR or decimal) to get the network address, broadcast, first and last usable IPs, the host count and the binary view.
ipv4.seoDescription: Free IPv4 calculator: network address, broadcast, host range, wildcard mask and CIDR ↔ decimal conversion, with a binary view. Great for networking classes.
about: An IPv4 network is defined by an address and a mask. The mask splits the network part (the fixed bits) from the host part (the bits that change from one machine to another). In CIDR notation, the mask is written as a slash followed by the number of network bits, for example /24.

This tool applies the mask to the address to derive the network address, the broadcast address, the first and last addresses you can assign to machines, the total number of usable hosts, the historical address class and the wildcard mask used in ACLs. The binary view colours the network and host bits so you can see the boundary.
examples: 10.0.0.1 /8 → network 10.0.0.0, broadcast 10.255.255.255, over 16 million hosts.
172.16.5.10 /30 → network 172.16.5.8, only 2 usable hosts (point-to-point link).

faq.q: What is the difference between /24 and 255.255.255.0?
faq.a: They are the same thing written differently: /24 means 24 network bits, which equals the decimal mask 255.255.255.0. The tool converts between both notations automatically.

faq.q: Why is the host count 2 less than the block size?
faq.a: In a classic subnet the first address is the network address and the last one is the broadcast: neither can be assigned to a machine, hence the minus two.
It is the binary inverse of the network mask (0s become 1s). It is mostly used in Cisco access control lists (ACLs).

base.name: Base converter (bin/oct/dec/hex)
base.short: Convert a number between binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal, with an ASCII table.
base.lead: Enter a value and pick its base: the tool instantly shows its conversion to binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal. A clickable ASCII table rounds it out.
base.seoDescription: Free base converter: binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal at a glance, with an ASCII table. Perfect for computer science and electronics.
about: A numeral base defines how many symbols are used to write a number: 2 in binary, 8 in octal, 10 in decimal and 16 in hexadecimal. The same number is therefore written differently depending on the base, but represents the same value.

Pick the base of your starting value and the tool immediately shows the other three representations. The ASCII table also lets you find a character's code and its spelling in each base, which is handy in computer science and digital electronics.
examples: 255 in decimal = 11111111 in binary = 377 in octal = FF in hexadecimal.
1010 in binary = 10 in decimal = A in hexadecimal.
The character 'A' has decimal code 65, that is 0x41 in hexadecimal.

faq.q: What is hexadecimal used for in computing?
faq.a: Hexadecimal is compact: two hex digits represent exactly one byte (8 bits). You find it in web colours (#FF8800), memory addresses and error codes.
Each base only accepts certain symbols: binary only 0 and 1, octal 0 to 7, hexadecimal 0 to 9 and A to F. A character outside that set is flagged as invalid.

base64.name: Base64 encoder / decoder
base64.short: Encode or decode text to and from Base64, right in your browser.
base64.lead: Paste or type your text, then encode it to Base64 or decode a Base64 string back to readable text. Everything happens locally in your browser.
base64.seoDescription: Encode and decode Base64 for free, online. Correct UTF-8 handling, 100% local processing in your browser, no data is ever sent.
about: Base64 encodes binary data using only 64 printable characters (letters, digits, + and /). It is used to carry content in formats that only accept text: emails, JSON, data URLs (data:) or authentication tokens.
Encoding increases the size by about a third and is not encryption: anyone can decode a Base64 string. This tool handles UTF-8 correctly (accents, emojis) and works entirely in your browser.
examples: 'Hello' encodes to 'SGVsbG8='.
'Qm9uam91cg==' decodes to 'Bonjour'.
An image can be embedded in a page via a data:image/png;base64,… URL.

faq.a: No. Base64 is reversible encoding, not encryption. Anyone can decode the string. To protect data you need real encryption.
No, encoding and decoding happen entirely in your browser. Nothing is transmitted to the server.

jwt.name: JWT decoder (JSON Web Token)
jwt.short: Decode a JWT's header and payload. 100% local, nothing is sent to the server.
jwt.lead: Paste a JSON Web Token to read its header, payload (claims) and check its issued and expiry dates. Decoding is entirely local.
jwt.seoDescription: Decode a JSON Web Token (JWT): header, payload, issued and expiry dates. A 100% local tool — the token is never sent to a server.
jwt.help: Paste a JSON Web Token below. Everything stays in your browser — the token is never sent to the server.
jwt.signatureNote: The signature is not verified in the browser (it would require the issuer's public key).
jwt.invalidFormat: A valid JWT has three segments separated by dots.
jwt.invalidContent: One of the segments could not be decoded as JSON.
about: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a string made of three parts separated by dots: a header, a payload (the claims) and a signature. The first two parts are simply Base64URL-encoded — so anyone can read them, this is not encryption.

This tool decodes the header and payload, and interprets the standard date fields (iat for issued-at, exp for expiry) to tell you whether the token is still valid. The signature itself guarantees integrity on the server side and cannot be verified without the issuer's key.
examples: A session token often contains a 'sub' field (the user id) and an 'exp' field (expiry date).
If the 'exp' date is in the past, the tool shows the 'Expired' badge.
The header segment reveals the signing algorithm, for example HS256 or RS256.

faq.q: Does decoding a JWT reveal secret information?
faq.a: A JWT's payload is only encoded, not encrypted: it is readable by anyone holding the token. So you should never put a password or sensitive data in it.

faq.q: Why is the signature not verified?
faq.a: Verifying the signature requires the issuer's secret key (HS256) or public key (RS256). This tool stays 100% local and has neither, so it decodes without validating the signature.

grade.name: Weighted grade calculator
grade.short: Compute your course average with coefficients, and the final diploma grade (TFE included).
grade.lead: Enter your grades and their weights to get your weighted average — with a diploma mode where the final project (TFE) counts for two thirds of the final grade.
grade.seoDescription: Compute your weighted grade average with coefficients and your final diploma grade (TFE = 2/3) for free. Online tool for students, out of 20 or 100.
grade.diplomaHint: The final grade combines the average of the retained courses and the final project (TFE) grade. By default the TFE counts for two thirds (⅔), but you can adjust this percentage to match your programme. Tick only the courses that count toward the diploma.
grade.diplomaFormula: Final grade = {{course}} % × retained courses average + {{tfe}} % × TFE
grade.tfeMissing: Enter the TFE grade to compute the final grade.
about: A weighted average takes each course's weight into account: a course with a coefficient of 3 counts three times as much as one with coefficient 1. The calculation sums each grade times its coefficient, then divides by the sum of coefficients. Leave every coefficient at 1 for a simple average.

Diploma mode combines the average of the retained courses and the final project (TFE) grade. You choose the TFE percentage (two thirds by default, as at ISFCE) and tick the courses that count — because not every course of a bachelor necessarily enters the diploma average.

The result also shows the distinction earned on the Belgian higher-education scale: pass with merit from 50 to 60%, satisfactory from 60 to 70%, distinction from 70 to 80%, high distinction from 80 to 90% and highest distinction from 90%. The pass threshold is 50% (i.e. 10/20).
examples: Two courses: 14 (weight 1) and 16 (weight 3) → weighted average = (14×1 + 16×3) / 4 = 15.5/20, a distinction (77.5%).
Default diploma mode: retained courses average 13/20 and TFE 16/20 → final grade = ⅓×13 + ⅔×16 = 15/20, a distinction (75%).
Set the TFE share to 50%: the final grade becomes the plain average of your retained courses and your TFE.

faq.q: How does the TFE weighting work?
faq.a: The TFE (final integrated project) carries a lot of weight in a bachelor. By default the tool gives it two thirds of the final grade and one third to the retained courses average, but you can change this percentage to match your programme or school.
Not every course of a bachelor necessarily enters the average that determines the diploma. In diploma mode, tick only the retained courses: only those are averaged before being combined with the TFE.

The tool follows the Belgian higher-education scale (ISFCE): below 50% = fail, 50 to 60% = pass with merit, 60 to 70% = satisfactory, 70 to 80% = distinction, 80 to 90% = high distinction, 90% and above = highest distinction.

faq.q: What should I put as a coefficient?
faq.a: Use each course's relative weight. If you do not know the official coefficients, leave them all at 1: you get a classic arithmetic average.

flashcards.name: Flashcards — revision cards
flashcards.short: Create your revision cards, study them with spaced repetition, and export them to Anki.
flashcards.lead: Create double-sided card decks, review them with spaced repetition, and export them in an Anki-compatible format. Everything stays in your browser — nothing is sent to a server.
flashcards.seoDescription: Create and review your revision cards with spaced repetition for free. Anki-compatible import/export, 100% in your browser, no sign-up.

flashcards.reviewTooltip: Review the cards due today (spaced repetition).
flashcards.nothingDue: Nothing due right now — click "Review all" to practise.
flashcards.libraryIntro: Decks shared by other verified students. Import one into "My decks" to review it — it's an editable copy, independent of the original.
about: Flashcards are one of the most effective ways to memorise: a question on the front, the answer on the back, and you self-test. Spaced repetition goes further — each card comes back to review just before you would forget it, anchoring the information in long-term memory with minimal effort.

This tool runs entirely in your browser: your cards are stored locally, nothing is sent to a server and no account is required. You can create several decks — one per course or chapter — and review only the cards due today.

On each card you rate your answer (Again, Hard, Good, Easy): the spaced-repetition algorithm then computes the next review, from a few minutes to several days away. You can also import a CSV/TSV file or export your cards in an Anki-compatible format to review on mobile.
examples: Create a "Networking — Subnetting" deck, add a card (front: "/26 mask?" → back: "255.255.255.192"), then start the review.
Import a file where each line holds the front, a tab, then the back: all cards are added at once.
Export your deck as .tsv and import it into Anki on your phone to revise on the go.

faq.q: Are my cards sent to a server?
faq.a: No. Everything is stored in your browser (localStorage). If you switch computers or clear your cache, export a JSON backup beforehand.

Yes, both ways. You can import an Anki deck (.apkg) directly to recover its basic cards. For export, the tool produces a tab-separated text file (TSV) that Anki imports natively: in Anki, choose File → Import, pick the file and map the first field to the front, the second to the back.

Each card has an interval that grows with every correct answer (1 day, then a few days, then longer). If you answer "Again", the card becomes due immediately. This is the principle of the SM-2 algorithm used by Anki.
Yes, as many as you like — one per course, chapter or exam. The selector at the top lets you switch between them.

quiz.name: Interactive quiz — build and share your MCQs
quiz.short: Build MCQs, play, share by link and climb the leaderboard.
quiz.lead: Build multiple-choice quizzes, practise, share them with classmates via a link and compare your scores on the leaderboard. Your quizzes stay in your browser — you decide when to publish them.
quiz.seoTitle: Online quiz & MCQ maker — create, share and play for free
quiz.seoDescription: Create your revision MCQs for free, share them by link and challenge your classmates on the leaderboard (score + speed). 100% in your browser, no sign-up to play.
quiz.errChoices: Each question needs at least two non-empty answers.
quiz.errAnswer: Pick the correct answer for each question (it can't be empty).
quiz.publishOk: Quiz published! It can now be played by other verified students.
quiz.shareTooLong: This quiz is large: the link is very long and may not work everywhere (messaging apps, etc.). Publish it to the library instead.
quiz.emptyHint: Create your first MCQ to practise and share it with your classmates.
quiz.sharedAtTooltip: A copy was published on {{date}} to the Library. Re-publishing creates a new copy.
quiz.libraryLoginHint: Sign in (verified ISFCE account) to play and publish shared quizzes.
quiz.libraryIntro: Quizzes shared by other verified students. Play, then compare your score on the leaderboard.
quiz.libraryEmpty: No shared quiz yet. Be the first to publish one!
quiz.leaderboardIntro: Best score per player — on a tie, the fastest wins.
quiz.leaderboardEmpty: No one has played yet. Give it a go!
quiz.submitError: Couldn't submit your score. Try again.
quiz.shareHint: Anyone can open this link and play, even without an account. The quiz is fully contained in the link — nothing is stored on the server, and it doesn't appear on the leaderboard.
about: A multiple-choice quiz (MCQ) is a fast, effective way to check what you know: read a question, pick the right answer among several, and get an instant score. Actively testing yourself cements memory far better than passively re-reading your notes.

This tool lets you build your own quizzes right in your browser, with no sign-up. You can play them as many times as you like, share them with classmates via a simple link, or publish them to the shared library so any verified student can practise on them.
Every published quiz has its own leaderboard: the best score per player is kept, and on a tie, speed decides. Perfect for revising an exam as a group in a friendly-challenge spirit.
examples: Build a "Networking — OSI layers" quiz with 10 questions, play it to self-assess, then share the link with your study group.
Publish your quiz to the library: your verified classmates play it and you compare your times on the leaderboard.
Generate a share link: even a classmate without an account can open the quiz and play it right away, with nothing to install.

faq.q: Do I need an account to play?
faq.a: To play a quiz shared by link, no — anyone can open it and answer. To publish a quiz to the shared library or record your score on the leaderboard, you need a verified ISFCE account.
In your browser (localStorage). Nothing is sent to the server until you click "Publish". Export a JSON backup before clearing your cache or switching devices.
Only your best score on each quiz is kept. On a tie, the faster player ranks higher. The score is computed on the server at submission, so the leaderboard stays reliable.

faq.q: Does the share link reveal the answers?
faq.a: A quiz shared by link is fully contained in the address: a curious user could technically decode it. That's harmless for a practice quiz, but for a reliable leaderboard, prefer publishing the quiz to the library (the answers then stay on the server).

about.metaDescription: Freenote is the free platform where ISFCE students share course notes, summaries, exercises and final projects. Discover the project's mission, how it works and its privacy stance.
about.orgDescription: Student platform for sharing documents (course notes, summaries, exercises, final projects) for ISFCE, in Charleroi, Belgium.
about.title: About Freenote
about.lead: Freenote is a free, independent platform that gathers the course notes, summaries, exercises and final projects of ISFCE students. The goal: that nothing gets lost and everyone revises from solid material.
mission: At ISFCE, like in many schools, student resources live scattered around: a PDF buried in a chat, a summary on a USB stick, a worked exercise nobody can find. Freenote centralises all of it, organised by section and course, so one cohort's work benefits the next.
The project was born within the ISFCE student community and remains an independent initiative: it is funded by discreet advertising and optional donations, never by selling data.

problems.title: Verifying students, simply
problems.desc: To protect the exchanges, only students with a verified @isfce.be address can access the documents. Verification is automatic: a code by email and you're done — no manual steps, no proof to show.

problems.title: Never lose anything again
problems.desc: Notes, summaries, exercises and final projects are organised by section and course, and stay available year after year — instead of vanishing into old conversations.

how.title: Sign in
how.desc: Create your account in one click via Discord, then choose your username and section.

how.title: Verify your ISFCE address
how.desc: Get a code on your @isfce.be address to unlock full access — and, as a bonus, the 'verified' role on the student Discord.

how.title: Explore and share
how.desc: Browse documents by course, open them right in the browser, and share your own to help your cohort and earn XP.

features.title: Documents by section and course
features.desc: Summaries, notes, exercises and final projects clearly sorted, with instant search.

features.title: In-browser reading
features.desc: PDFs open directly on the site, with no forced download and no sign-up to a third-party service.

features.title: Leaderboard and XP
features.desc: Every shared document earns points: a leaderboard highlights the most generous students.

features.title: Free tools
features.desc: A weighted grade calculator, an IPv4 calculator, a base converter and other handy tools, no account needed.

privacy: Freenote keeps only what's necessary: your Discord id, your @isfce.be address as a hash (never in clear text), the username and profile you fill in, and the documents you upload. PDF files are never exposed publicly: they only pass through the server, for verified accounts.
You can stay anonymous on the documents you share, keep your profile private, and delete your account at any time. The project's code is open and available on GitHub.

faq.a: Yes, entirely. Discreet advertising and optional donations (Ko-fi) fund the hosting; a donation removes the ads for 30 days.
Students with a verified @isfce.be address. The public pages (home, tools, news, legal notices) stay open to everyone.

faq.q: Is Freenote official or affiliated with ISFCE?
faq.a: No. It is an independent student initiative, with no official link to the school.

faq.q: How do I share a document?
faq.a: Once your address is verified, click 'Share': pick the section, course and category, then drop a PDF or photos (they are merged into a single PDF).

about.ctaText: Join the ISFCE students who revise better thanks to shared resources.
